adds.title: LGBT rights in Nigeria - Wikipedia
adds.summary: Wikipedia's Nigeria LGBT-rights overview records that same-sex sexual activity has been illegal across the country since 1916 and that the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act — passed by the House of Representatives on 30 May 2013 and signed into law by President Goodluck Jonathan in January 2014 — criminalises all forms of same-sex unions, rendering any marriage or civil union entered into between persons of the same sex invalid and void. It states the maximum penalty under federal law is up to 14 years' imprisonment, with the death penalty confined to the twelve northern states operating Shari'a-based criminal codes, and that in the southern portion of the country, which includes Akwa Ibom, the maximum punishment for same-sex sexual activity is 14 years' imprisonment. The page also records no legal recognition of gender identity, no anti-discrimination protections and no recognition of same-sex relationships. This is the national-framework source for the record's claim that the 2014 statute punishes same-sex unions in Akwa Ibom with up to 14 years' imprisonment.

adds.title: Country policy and information note: sexual orientation, gender identity and expression, and sex characteristics, Nigeria, June 2025 (accessible) - GOV.UK
adds.summary: The UK Home Office's June 2025 country policy and information note on Nigeria documents the national criminal framework on sexual orientation and gender identity that applies across all states, including the 2014 statute punishing same-sex unions, and records countrywide harm patterns of arrests, detention and mob violence against LGBT+ people. It confirms that the twelve northern states' Shari'a penal codes — with penalties for same-sex conduct from lashes or caning up to death by stoning — remain in force, citing a Shari'a court in Bauchi sentencing three men to death by stoning in 2022, a sentence that could not be carried out until ratified by the state governor, a further report of a death-by-stoning sentence from Bauchi in May 2024, and a January 2014 incident in which a mob stormed a Bauchi court demanding death during a sodomy trial. This confirms that the death-penalty risk layer is confined to the northern Shari'a states and does not extend to southern states such as Akwa Ibom, which stands under the secular national 14-year framework — matching this record's position that no state-specific enforcement divergence is documented.
